title: The Slow Museum, the Valdoria Metro, and the 15-Minute City: A Simulated Academic Reading Test
instructions: 本材料为模拟学术英语阅读练习，不隶属任何官方考试，也不代表任何官方分数。阅读部分共三篇文章，总词数约2400词，请按题目顺序作答。选择题每题只有一个正确答案；填空题答案必须与原文完全一致，且不超过规定的词数；判断题请选择 True、False 或 Not Given。所有答案和解析在完成后查看。建议用时：60分钟。

PASSAGE 1

A

The town of Marlow-on-Sea had been known for decades as a quiet retirement destination. Its promenade was lined with small hotels, and its museum, housed in a former fishing warehouse, attracted only a few hundred visitors each year. In 2019, however, the town council approved a plan that would change the museum’s fortunes. The plan, known as the Slow Museum Project, was designed by a team of curators and local historians who believed that visitors should be given time to think rather than being hurried through exhibitions. Under the new scheme, the museum would open only four days a week, and each visitor would be limited to a two-hour session. Tickets would be sold in advance, and the number of people allowed inside at any one time would be capped at forty. The team argued that a calmer, more controlled environment would allow the museum to compete with larger attractions by offering something they could not: the chance to look properly at a small, carefully arranged collection.

B

The decision was not universally welcomed. Several councillors argued that reducing opening hours would damage the town’s tourism income. They pointed out that the museum had previously been free to enter and that charging for timed tickets might discourage families. The project team responded by explaining that the two-hour limit was not intended to restrict visitors but to encourage them to focus. “When people know they have only two hours,” said Dr. Ellen Marsh, the project’s lead curator, “they tend to spend more time on each object instead of rushing past everything.” The council eventually agreed to a twelve-month trial, after which the scheme would be reviewed. The debate reflected a wider tension in the town between those who saw tourism as a source of income and those who saw the museum as a place of learning.

C

The first year of the trial produced surprising results. Although the total number of visitors fell by about fifteen per cent, the average time each visitor spent inside the museum rose from twenty-five minutes to nearly ninety minutes. More importantly, surveys conducted at the exit showed that visitors remembered significantly more details about the exhibits than they had in previous years. The museum’s shop also reported a thirty per cent increase in sales, which the manager attributed to the fact that visitors were leaving in a more reflective mood and were therefore more willing to browse. Staff noted that visitors asked more questions and lingered longer in front of individual displays, suggesting that the slower format had changed behaviour rather than merely reducing numbers.

D

Encouraged by these findings, the council decided to extend the trial for a further two years. During this period, the museum was able to secure additional funding from a regional heritage fund. The money was used to create a new gallery devoted to the town’s fishing history, and to install interactive screens that allowed visitors to explore the museum’s collection at their own pace. The screens were designed so that they could be used by people with limited mobility, and they were placed at a height that made them accessible to children as well as adults. The new gallery quickly became the most popular part of the museum, and school groups began to book visits months in advance.

E

Not everything went smoothly. In the second year of the extended trial, the museum was forced to close for three weeks when a storm damaged part of its roof. The closure cost the museum an estimated £18,000 in lost ticket sales. In addition, some local residents complained that the advance booking system made it difficult for them to visit spontaneously. The museum responded by reserving a small number of tickets for walk-in visitors each day, although these were often snapped up within minutes of opening. The roof was eventually repaired with the help of a local fundraising campaign, which itself strengthened the museum’s ties with the community.

F

By the end of the third year, the Slow Museum Project had become a model for other small museums in the region. Representatives from six neighbouring towns visited Marlow-on-Sea to observe the scheme, and two of them subsequently introduced similar timed-entry systems. Dr. Marsh, however, warns against copying the model without adaptation. “The two-hour limit works here because our collection is small and focused,” she explains. “A larger museum with a much bigger collection might need a different approach. The principle is to give visitors permission to slow down, not to impose a fixed time on everyone.” Her warning has been widely quoted in discussions of museum management.

G

Looking ahead, the museum plans to introduce a series of evening events aimed at local workers who cannot visit during the day. These events will combine short talks by historians with the opportunity to explore the galleries after hours. The council has also agreed to fund a part-time education officer, whose role will be to develop resources for school groups. It is hoped that these initiatives will strengthen the museum’s relationship with the local community and secure its long-term future. The museum’s director has said that the project has changed not only how the museum works but how the town thinks about its own history.

PASSAGE 2

A

When the city of Valdoria decided to build a new metro line, the initial plan was drawn up by engineers who had little experience of working in densely populated areas. The proposed route ran directly beneath the old market square, a site that had been used for public gatherings for over three centuries. Local historians and residents objected strongly, arguing that the construction work would damage the foundations of the surrounding buildings and destroy the square’s unique atmosphere. The engineers, however, insisted that the route was the most efficient and that any damage could be repaired afterwards. They pointed to the cost savings and the shorter journey times that the direct route would deliver.

B

The dispute was eventually resolved by the intervention of the city’s mayor, who commissioned an independent review. The review concluded that while the engineers’ route was technically feasible, it failed to take into account the social and cultural value of the square. It recommended that the line be rerouted to pass beneath a nearby industrial area that was scheduled for redevelopment. This alternative route was slightly longer and would cost an additional €40 million, but it would avoid the market square entirely. The mayor accepted the recommendation, and the revised plan was approved by the city council in 2021. The decision was seen as a victory for those who argued that infrastructure should serve communities rather than the other way round.

C

Construction began in early 2022. The project was divided into three phases, each lasting approximately eighteen months. The first phase involved digging a deep trench along the industrial area and reinforcing the walls with concrete. This work was carried out by a team of 200 workers, many of whom had been recruited from the local area. The second phase, which began in mid-2023, focused on the tunnel itself. A massive boring machine, nicknamed “the Mole” by the workers, was assembled on site and slowly moved forward, cutting through the earth and installing the tunnel lining as it went. The machine operated day and night, and its progress was followed with interest by local residents.

D

The third phase, still ongoing at the time of writing, involves the construction of the stations. The design of the stations was influenced by feedback from a series of public consultations held in 2022. Residents asked for more natural light, better signage, and spaces for local artists to display their work. As a result, the stations will feature large skylights, digital information screens, and dedicated exhibition walls. The station at the industrial area, which will be the largest on the line, will also include a small park on its roof. The architects hope that the stations will feel like public buildings rather than purely functional spaces.

E

One of the biggest challenges has been managing the impact of construction on local businesses. Shops along the route have experienced reduced footfall because of road closures and noise. To address this, the city introduced a compensation scheme that offers grants to affected businesses. In addition, a temporary pedestrian bridge was built over the construction site to allow shoppers to reach the main shopping street. The bridge, which was designed by a local architect, has been praised for its bright colours and has itself become something of a landmark. Some shopkeepers remain concerned about the long-term effects, but most agree that the city has responded more openly than they had expected.

F

When the line opens, scheduled for late 2026, it is expected to reduce journey times between the industrial area and the city centre by up to twenty minutes. The city hopes that the new line will encourage the redevelopment of the industrial area, which has been largely abandoned for over a decade. Plans for the area include new housing, offices, and a riverside walk. However, some critics warn that the new housing will be too expensive for local people and that the area may lose its distinctive character. The city has promised that a proportion of the new homes will be affordable, though the exact figure has not yet been confirmed.

G

Reflecting on the project, the mayor said that the most important lesson had been the value of listening. “We could have saved money by ignoring the objections,” she admitted. “But we would have lost something far more valuable: the trust of the people who live here.” The Valdoria metro line is now cited in urban planning courses as an example of how infrastructure projects can be designed with communities rather than imposed upon them. The mayor added that the early consultations had cost time but had ultimately saved the city from far more expensive disputes later.

PASSAGE 3

A

The concept of the “15-minute city” has gained considerable attention in recent years. Put simply, it is an urban planning model in which residents can reach all essential services—shops, schools, healthcare, parks, and workplaces—within a fifteen-minute walk or cycle from their homes. The idea was popularised by Professor Carlos Moreno, who argued that cities should be designed around the needs of people rather than cars. According to Moreno, the 15-minute city is not simply about reducing travel time; it is about improving quality of life by creating vibrant, mixed-use neighbourhoods. The model has been taken up by mayors and planners in many countries as a response to congestion, pollution, and the isolation of modern urban life.

B

Supporters of the model point to several potential benefits. First, it is argued that shorter journeys will lead to reduced carbon emissions and less traffic congestion. Second, by encouraging people to walk and cycle, the model may improve public health. Third, it is claimed that local businesses will benefit because residents will spend more time and money in their own neighbourhoods. Finally, proponents suggest that stronger community bonds will develop as people interact more frequently with their neighbours. These benefits are often presented as mutually reinforcing, with each improvement making the others more likely.

C

However, the 15-minute city has also attracted criticism. Some commentators argue that the model is unrealistic in rural areas, where services are naturally spread out and public transport is limited. Others point out that creating mixed-use neighbourhoods may lead to rising property prices, which could force lower-income residents out of the very areas that are being improved. This process, known as gentrification, has been observed in several cities that have adopted similar policies. A further concern is that the model may be used to justify reducing investment in public transport, on the assumption that people will not need to travel far. Critics argue that this would disadvantage those who cannot walk or cycle, including the elderly and people with disabilities.

D

Several cities have attempted to put the 15-minute city into practice. In Paris, for example, the mayor has introduced a series of measures aimed at reducing car use and creating more green spaces. School playgrounds have been opened to the public outside school hours, and some streets have been pedestrianised. In Melbourne, a pilot project in a suburb called Fitzroy North involved mapping local services and identifying gaps. The mapping exercise revealed that while the area had plenty of cafes and shops, it lacked affordable childcare and a medical centre. As a result, the local council has prioritised these services in its planning decisions. The project has since been extended to other suburbs.

E

One of the most detailed experiments has been in the city of Utrecht in the Netherlands. A neighbourhood called Merwede is being redeveloped according to 15-minute principles. The plan includes a car-free centre, extensive cycle paths, and a mix of housing types. Importantly, the developers have committed to ensuring that at least thirty per cent of the housing is affordable. They have also involved residents in the design process through a series of workshops. According to the project’s director, this participatory approach has been crucial in building trust and ensuring that the development meets the needs of the people who will live there. The first residents are expected to move in within the next two years.

F

Despite these examples, measuring the success of the 15-minute city is not straightforward. There is no single agreed set of indicators. Some researchers focus on the proportion of residents who can reach key services within fifteen minutes, while others emphasise changes in travel behaviour or levels of community satisfaction. Moreover, the fifteen-minute threshold itself is somewhat arbitrary; what matters, many argue, is not the exact time but the principle of proximity. As one urban planner put it, “The fifteen-minute city is a direction of travel, not a destination.” This view suggests that the model should be judged by whether it moves cities in the right direction rather than by whether every resident can reach every service within a quarter of an hour.

G

Looking to the future, the model is likely to be adapted rather than adopted wholesale. Different cities have different histories, densities, and cultures, and what works in Utrecht may not work in a sprawling suburb of a large metropolis. The most successful examples appear to be those in which local people have been actively involved in shaping the plans. As Moreno himself has acknowledged, the 15-minute city is not a fixed blueprint but a set of principles that must be translated into local contexts. Planners therefore need to ask not whether a city is a 15-minute city, but how the principles of proximity and participation can be applied to its particular conditions.

H

In conclusion, the 15-minute city offers a compelling vision of urban life, but it is not without its challenges. It requires careful planning, significant investment, and a willingness to listen to residents. It also demands a shift in how we think about time and distance. Whether it will become the dominant model of urban development in the twenty-first century remains to be seen, but its influence on planning debates is already considerable. For now, it serves as a useful test of whether a city is designed for people or for vehicles, and that question is unlikely to disappear.

grammar.title: 被动语态、顺序与地点表达、变化表达及句子间衔接
grammar.explanation: 本练习重点复习四类结构：1）被动语态（be + 过去分词），用于强调动作承受者或未知执行者；2）顺序与地点表达（first, then, finally; beneath, along, on its roof 等）；3）变化表达（rise from...to..., increase by..., fall by...）；4）句子间衔接（however, in addition, as a result, moreover 等）。请根据语境选择最恰当的形式。
grammar.example: the average time each visitor spent inside the museum rose from twenty-five minutes to nearly ninety minutes

questions.prompt: Choose the correct option: The new gallery ______ by a local architect last year.
questions.explanation: 主语gallery是动作承受者，且时间last year表示过去，故用一般过去时被动语态was designed。
questions.evidence: The money was used to create a new gallery

questions.prompt: Choose the correct option: First, the trench was dug. ______, the tunnel was constructed.
questions.explanation: 此处表示时间顺序，先挖沟，然后建隧道，故用Then。
questions.evidence: The first phase involved digging a deep trench ... The second phase ... focused on the tunnel itself.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct option: The number of visitors fell ______ about fifteen per cent.
questions.explanation: 表示下降幅度用fall by + 百分比；fall to表示降至某数值。
questions.evidence: the total number of visitors fell by about fifteen per cent

questions.prompt: Choose the correct option: The station will include a small park ______ its roof.
questions.explanation: 表示在屋顶表面用介词on。
questions.evidence: will also include a small park on its roof
